before: class defines a class; Counter.new(2) allocates an instance and calls its initialize method with 2. initialize sets up that instance rather than returning the new object itself.

@value is an instance variable belonging to the current receiver. value += 1 means add one and store the result; here @value += 1 updates that receiver. A method returns its last expression, so advance returns the updated number.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
class Counter
  def initialize(start)
    @value = start
  end
  def advance
    @value += 1
  end
end
first = Counter.new(2)
second = Counter.new(8)
puts first.advance
puts second.advance
```

Expected output or behavior: 3
9. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

The at-sign name belongs to the object receiving the method call.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
class Counter
  def initialize(start)
    @value = start
  end
  def advance
    @value += 1
  end
end
first = Counter.new(2)
second = Counter.new(8)
puts first.advance
puts second.advance
```
The output is `3`, then `9`. The two separate counters advance from two and eight.
